posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

And here we thought spiders and insects are Australia's biggest threat... 😬

Back in 1932, Australia went to war against the most unusual enemy. It wasn't another country or an invading army. It was a flock of 20,000 emus! They invaded and devastated farmers' wheat fields and the government had no other option but to take out the big guns, literally. What followed has since become one of the strangest military operations in the history: the Great Emu War.

Watch our latest Nightshift video to find out what actually happened during the Emu War, how one of the world's larg

On the vast, cold seas with endless waves in all directions, there is one constant companion: the stars. Whenever they were visible, sailors knew they could find their way. Their guidance meant ships could dare to cross the oceans with nothing more than keen eyesight and the ability to read the signs in the sky. Just like the brave sailors aboard Chinese junks that can be seen on the July page of our 12,026 Human Era calendar, who left familiar shores to cross oceans and head into the unknown.

War costs far more than weapons and destroyed buildings. It leaves countries poorer, disrupts education, drives migration, and passes trauma to future generations. Some of its highest costs are paid decades later.

Hidden in the tropical rainforest of Queensland, Australia, Paronella Park is a historic Spanish-style castle built by José Paronella in the 1930s. Surrounded by lush gardens, waterfalls, and ancient trees, this unique destination feels like a forgotten piece of another world.⁠
⁠
Thanks to @ourtropicaltribe for showing us this incredible gem of @tropicalnorthqueensland.

This island is home to three of the world’s most unique seabirds. ⁠
⁠
Located in Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands, North Seymour Island is a small volcanic island where blue-footed, red-footed, and Nazca boobies all thrive.⁠
⁠
It’s one of the rare places where you can see these incredible birds sharing the same habitat in the wild.⁠
⁠
Would you visit this island? 🌎

The Lithium Crystal Sauna was built in WasteLand Climate Action Park, a place that transformed a former industrial site into a public space for art, nature, and community.⁠
⁠
Its crystal-inspired design pays tribute to the region's history, while the project itself shows how landscapes can take on a completely new purpose over time.⁠
⁠
By: @studiobigertbergstrom @parolofsson

An Airbnb where your roommate is a warthog named Pumba!🐗⁠
That's right! Found in Namibia, Africa, this stay is an experience unlike any other.⁠
⁠
🎥: @vivienwallmerier

In the Canary Islands, there’s a retreat that slows you down before you even arrive. ⁠
⁠
To request a stay at El Elevador, guests send a handwritten letter explaining why they want to visit. Each letter is read personally, and if accepted, guests receive a handwritten letter by post, followed by the instructions to complete their booking.⁠
⁠
The stay is limited to 2 guests to keep it quiet and personal. ⁠
⁠
By: @el_elevador

These aren’t generic info pages. You get the direct contact of the exact person who approves collabs at each hotel - the marketing and PR managers who decide who stays for free and who gets paid.

500 hotels, all over the world, updated constantly.

You don’t need more followers. You need the right list and the right person to email.

Follow @travelcreator.club for the system behind it.

They may be smaller than a sparrow, but sociable weaver birds create some of the most impressive structures in the animal world. ⁠
⁠
Found across southern Africa, these tiny birds build enormous communal nests that can stretch up to 20 feet wide and provide a home for hundreds of birds at once.⁠
⁠
The nests are more than just a place to rest. Their unique design helps the birds handle the region’s extreme temperatures, keeping them protected from cold desert nights and intense daytime heat.

The Bernina Express winds through the Alps at a slower pace, giving you time to take in glaciers, mountain villages, alpine lakes, and some of Europe's most incredible scenery.⁠
⁠
It's easy to see why so many people consider it one of the world's most beautiful train journeys.⁠
⁠
Would you add it to your travel bucket list? 🌍 ⁠
⁠
By: @gross.oskar @alixgreenman @alexciland

Hvítserkur is a 15-meter-tall basalt sea stack on Iceland's Vatnsnes Peninsula, shaped by thousands of years of wind, waves, and erosion.⁠
⁠
But locals tell a different story. According to Icelandic folklore, it was once a troll that stayed out too late and was turned to stone by the sunrise. Depending on where you're standing, you might see a dragon, a dinosaur, or even a giant rhinoceros. Either way, it's one of those places that's even more impressive in person.⁠
⁠

This is one of the world’s most extreme train journeys that crosses the Sahara Desert.⁠
⁠
The Iron Ore Train runs between the mining town of Zouérat and the coastal city of Nouadhibou, traveling for more than 20 hours through one of the harshest landscapes on Earth.⁠
⁠

Can you find the gecko?

Photographer @chienleephotography photographed this mossy leaf-tailed gecko (Uroplatus sikorae) hiding in plain sight in Mantadia National Park, Madagascar. These geckos have uncanny camouflaging abilities, which are needed in a rainforest filled with keen-eyed predators. When resting, they face downward to catch unsuspecting insects climbing from the ground and to prevent their eyes from reflecting light that can alert birds to their presence.

Have you ever seen an orca ram a sunfish so hard that it was smashed to bits? This incredible footage of one orca holding the fish by the tail while another rammed it was captured by marine biologist and National Geographic Explorer Katy Ayres, and it raises several questions about the purpose of this behavior. Sunfish are the heaviest bony fish on the planet, but an orca can easily kill them, leading some researchers to theorize it may be a game rather than a hunting tactic.

You know the story: Mount Vesuvius erupts, Pompeii vanishes, thousands perish. But 2,000 years later, history’s most famous disaster is telling us something new.

In the cover story of our August issue, out now, we explore how AI and advanced DNA analysis are answering questions archaeologists could once only guess at. A cache of charred scrolls is readable again thanks to a pioneering virtual "unwrapping" technology. Newly excavated toilets at Pompeii have sparked a groundbreaking genomic study

For sperm whales to live well, they must be heard. Whether diving to forage or chatting at the surface, or supporting each other through childbirth, they communicate through energetic, rhythmical sequences of clicks called codas. But the ocean is far from silent, especially as human activities like underwater drilling and shipping increase. New research from @projectceti, a multidisciplinary initiative aiming to translate sperm whale communication, suggests shipping noise is changing the message

Photo by @joelsartore | This juvenile Andean fox will play a vital role throughout its life in helping many of the plants and animals within its home range to thrive. As a skilled predator, it will aid in population control by feeding on small mammals, reptiles, and insects. Andean foxes also eat fruit, making them important seed dispersers of peumo fruit and Peruvian peppers. This photo was taken @ufas_unab. Trauma doesn't just affect the people who experience it. Studies suggest that negative life-changing experiences can alter our genes in ways that are passed down to the next generation, leading to an increased risk of conditions like depression, anxiety, and PTSD.

Learn more about the research at the link in bio. 

Photograph by Tek Image, Science Photo Library

Photographer Jennifer Adler (@jmadler) photographed this young harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) near the Hopkins Marine Station in Monterey, California. Seals are known for their curious and playful demeanor, but they can also easily become stressed with unexpected human interaction. Their presence typically indicates a healthy habitat, as they consume fish that are vulnerable to pollution, in turn regulating their populations.

A mouthful of teeth 🦁🦷

30 to be precise. As predators and carnivores, lions use their teeth to hunt and eat. They have twelve incisors, four canines, ten premolars and four molars for gripping prey and cutting meat.

#EarthCapture by @jackswynnerton

Waiting for the perfect moment 🐆
 
Perched high above the ground, the leopard waits until an impala comes within striking distance. After staying completely still, it launches from the tree in one powerful leap, but will all that patience pay off?
 
Celebrate 20 years of Planet Earth with us. Find out where to watch the full episode via our link in bio 💚

#PlanetEarth #DavidAttenborough #PE20 #PEIII

How do you attract a female? 🦌🦕

The most attractive are usually the biggest and hairiest with prominent features. In reproduction, they pass their genes to the next generation, who inherit more exaggerated attributes. Over millions of years, animal traits modify for better mating chances.

Find out where to watch Evolution via the link in our bio 🔗💚

#Evolution #ChrisPackham #Nature

Someone’s got serious aim 🎯
 
An archerfish doesn’t chase its prey. Instead, it fires a powerful jet of water with remarkable precision, knocking unsuspecting insects straight into the water. One perfectly placed shot is all it takes before the fish darts in to claim its meal. 
 
Celebrate 20 years of Planet Earth with us. Find out where to watch the full episode via our link in bio 💚

#PlanetEarth #DavidAttenborough #PE20 #PEIII

Penises come in all shapes and sizes 🍆

Shells prevented reptiles from fertilising their eggs, yet evolution created a solution: the penis. Reptiles were among the first animals to have them, but they weren’t the last. For life on land, it meant sex as we know it had been invented.

Find out where to watch Evolution via the link in our bio 🔗💚

#Evolution #ChrisPackham #Nature

🦦 Otter vs otter 🦦

Despite their cute reputation, fierce otter fights aren’t uncommon. Clashes over territories, food supplies and mating disputes can break out and become intense. Some end in serious injury, or even death.

It’s World Chimpanzee Day 🐵

Chimps share DNA with humans, but Dr Jane Goodall discovered other similarities making them our closest living relatives. They use tools, hold hands, embrace one another and use non-verbal communication like humans too.

Warthog snouts are survival tools 🐗

It’s used for sniffing, digging and foraging, but they must bend their legs to reach the ground. Another creature evolved a longer snout for the same purpose, and it developed a body shape we recognise today.
